opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think "niche" is a bit of a relative word here. If you look at it from the perspective of the overall consumer internet, sure, 3D content creation is smaller than, say, short video or social apps. But for a startup, that's actually a feature, not a bug.

A few reasons. First, the technical barrier is high. Building good 3D tools requires deep expertise in graphics, simulation, geometry, compilers, and now machine learning. That's not something a big company can just throw a hundred generalist engineers at and solve in six months. When I was working on Taichi during my PhD, I realized how few people really understand the full stack, from the math down to the GPU. That scarcity of talent and know-how is a natural moat for a small, focused team.

Second, the demand side is growing much faster than people assume. Games, film, e-commerce, AR/VR, robotics, digital twins: all of these need 3D assets, and the traditional pipeline is painfully slow and expensive. An artist might spend days or even weeks on a single high-quality model. So there's a huge gap between how much 3D content the world wants and how much it can actually produce. Whenever you see that kind of gap, there's room for a new tool to come in and change the economics.

Third, timing. With generative AI, we're at a point where the technology is just becoming good enough to make 3D creation dramatically more accessible. Big companies tend to move cautiously in markets that don't look huge yet. That gives a startup a window to move fast, iterate with real users, and build something that becomes the default before the market becomes obviously big.

So I'd say it's a classic startup story: start in a place that looks small, where you have a real technical edge, and grow with the market as it expands. I'd much rather be a leader in a market that's going to explode than be the hundredth player in a crowded space.

r001.rationale: The response mentions that large companies may move cautiously in small markets and that crowded spaces are less appealing, but it does not identify competition from large companies as a reason very large markets can be unsuitable for startups.

r002.rationale: It calls the niche market small relative to consumer internet and says startups can grow with it; it does not state that a market may be too small to sustain a startup.

r003.rationale: The response favors starting in a niche or small market, but does not identify a medium-sized market as favorable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd actually push back a little on the word "niche." 3D looks small today because it's hard, not because nobody wants it. Almost everything physical around us was designed in 3D, every game and film you watch is built in 3D, and robotics, AR, simulation, e-commerce are all pulling in the same direction. The demand is enormous. What's tiny is the number of people who can actually produce 3D content, because the tools demand years of training and the pipelines are painful. That gap between huge latent demand and a tiny supply of creators is exactly where a startup wants to be.

The second reason is that it's a hard, technical problem, and hard problems are good for small teams. If the problem were easy, a big company would have already solved it. Big companies are great at scaling things that work, but they're bad at the messy, multi-year grind where you have to combine graphics, compilers, physics simulation, and now generative AI, and no single org owns all of those pieces. My background is in exactly that intersection. I spent my PhD building Taichi, which is a language for high-performance physical simulation, and I saw up close how much friction there is between what researchers can do and what practitioners can use. A startup can live in that gap and move fast.

The third reason is timing. For a long time the bottleneck was compute and algorithms. Now you have GPUs everywhere, differentiable rendering, neural representations, and generative models that can plausibly produce geometry and materials from a sentence or a photo. When the cost of creating something drops by a hundred x, markets that looked niche become mainstream. That's what happened with photography, with video, with 2D design once tools like Figma and Canva showed up. 3D hasn't had its moment yet, and whoever builds the tool that makes a non-expert productive in 3D gets to define that market.

And honestly, being niche early is an advantage, not a liability. It means we can go deep with a specific set of users, understand their workflow in detail, and build something they genuinely love, rather than something that's a little bit useful to everyone. You earn the right to expand from there.

r001.rationale: It says large companies struggle with messy, technical problems, but does not say very large markets are unsuitable because of competition from them.

r002.rationale: It argues that 3D has enormous demand despite seeming small; it does not say a market can be too small to sustain a startup.

r003.rationale: It favors a niche market as an early advantage, but does not identify a medium-sized market as favorable.

astra-6.text:
I think a startup doesn’t necessarily need to start in the biggest market. It needs to find a problem that matters a lot to a group of users and solve it substantially better than the alternatives. In a huge, established market, you’re often competing with companies that have far more resources. A niche can give a small team room to develop a real advantage.

With 3D, there’s a lot of technical complexity, and creating content can require considerable time and expertise. That creates opportunities to make the workflow easier and more accessible. If you lower those barriers, you’re not just competing for existing users—you can help more people become users.

So I’d distinguish between a market that’s small because demand is limited and one that’s small because participation is difficult. I think 3D has a lot of the second characteristic. That makes it an interesting place to start.

r001.rationale: It says startups in huge, established markets often compete with companies that have far more resources.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes markets with limited demand from markets constrained by participation, but does not state that a market can be too small to sustain a startup.

r003.rationale: It describes a niche market as an interesting place to start, but does not identify a medium-sized market as favorable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a niche market can be a very good starting point if there’s a difficult problem that people really need solved. In 3D, creating high-quality content takes a lot of time and expertise. If a startup can make that process substantially easier, it can offer clear value even to a relatively small group of users.

And the opportunity isn’t necessarily limited to the market as it exists today. If you lower the barrier to creating 3D content, more people can use it, and new applications become possible. So I would look at both the depth of the problem today and the potential for the market to grow as the technology improves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the value of solving a difficult problem in 3D, but does not mention competition with large companies.

r002.rationale: It says a niche market can serve a relatively small group, but does not state that a market can be too small to sustain a startup.

r003.rationale: It favors a niche market as a starting point, but does not identify a medium-sized market as favorable.
